sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Case-study questions test whether you can translate abstract system design knowledge into a working architecture for a specific product. Go engineers are frequently asked to design URL shorteners, rate limiters, chat systems, job queues, and API gateways because these are real services that appear in every backend stack. Answering well demonstrates both design breadth and Go-specific implementation fluency.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: Each case study follows the same arc: (1) Clarify scope and constraints (read vs. write ratio, latency SLO). (2) Sketch the happy-path data flow. (3) Identify the bottleneck (storage, CPU, network). (4) Apply the right distributed-systems primitive (consistent hashing, pub/sub, token bucket). (5) Harden with failure modes. In Go, map the primitives to concrete packages: net/http for the gateway, goroutines + channels for the queue, sync.Mutex + time.Ticker for in-process rate limiting.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: URL Shortener: base62 encoding, collision avoidance, 301 vs. 302 redirect, read-heavy caching. Rate Limiter: token bucket algorithm, Redis INCR + EXPIRE for distributed counters, golang.org/x/time/rate for local limiting. Chat System: WebSocket in Go (gorilla/websocket or nhooyr.io/websocket), fan-out to subscribers, message ordering with sequence IDs. Job Queue: producer/consumer with buffered channels, dead-letter queue, at-least-once vs. exactly-once delivery, idempotency keys. API Gateway: reverse proxy (httputil.ReverseProxy), auth middleware, circuit breaker (sony/gobreaker), request routing.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: • 'Design a URL shortener that handles 100 k reads/s.' → cache-aside with Redis, base62 ID generation, CDN for 301 redirects. • 'How would you implement a rate limiter as a shared library in Go?' → golang.org/x/time/rate, sync.Map per tenant, Redis fallback for multi-process. • 'Design a real-time chat system for 1 M concurrent users.' → WebSocket goroutines, pub/sub (Redis or NATS), horizontal scaling with consistent hashing for room affinity. • 'How does your job queue handle retries and poison messages?' → exponential back-off, dead-letter queue, idempotency key stored in Redis.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "Let me start with the URL shortener. My first question is: what's the read-to-write ratio? Typically it's 100:1, which means I should heavily optimise for reads. I'd store the short-to-long mapping in PostgreSQL for durability, layer Redis in front for hot URLs, and serve a 301 redirect so browsers cache it client-side. For ID generation I'd use base62 on a 64-bit counter from a distributed ID service to avoid collisions. The Go service itself is stateless—just a net/http handler that looks up Redis, falls through to Postgres, and issues the redirect. Scaling is purely horizontal behind a load balancer."
